target_report.plain_explanation: Prisma maintains a pool of persistent database connections. Use a global singleton pattern to prevent duplicate intervals: 'declare global { var _cleanupInterval: NodeJS.Timeout | undefined; } if (globalThis._cleanupInterval) clearInterval(globalThis._cleanupInterval); globalThis._cleanupInterval = setInterval(async () => { await cleanupExpiredSessions(); }, 60_000);'. Alternatively, only start the scheduler on the first invocation using a guard flag. Do not run scheduled jobs in edge functions.
verification_steps: Apply the globalThis singleton pattern to the scheduler.
Save a file multiple times to trigger HMR and verify the job fires only once per interval.
Monitor process memory to confirm it no longer grows continuously during development.

review.review_notes: Synthetic Zustand persist middleware causing Next.js hydration mismatch on first render.

model_input.raw_error:
Error: Hydration failed because the initial UI does not match what was rendered on the server.
Warning: Prop 'className' did not match. Server: 'theme-light' Client: 'theme-dark'
    at ThemeWrapper (src/components/ThemeWrapper.tsx:9:5)

context.recent_changes: Added Zustand persist middleware with localStorage to store user theme preference.

reference_annotations.reference_cause: Zustand persist reads from localStorage during client hydration, but server-side rendering has no localStorage access so the server renders the default value while the client renders the persisted value.
reference_annotations.reference_repair: Use Zustand's built-in 'skipHydration' option and manually call 'useStore.persist.rehydrate()' inside a useEffect to delay localStorage reads until after hydration.

target_report.summary: Zustand persist causes a hydration mismatch because localStorage is unavailable on the server but provides a different value on the client.
target_report.plain_explanation: Zustand's persist middleware saves and restores state from localStorage. During server-side rendering, localStorage does not exist, so the store initializes with the default value (e.g. 'light' theme). When the page hydrates in the browser, Zustand reads the persisted 'dark' theme from localStorage. React detects that the rendered HTML ('theme-light') differs from what client hydration produces ('theme-dark') and throws a hydration error.

likely_causes.description: Zustand persist middleware restores state from localStorage during client hydration, differing from the server-rendered default value.
The component renders different classNames based on persisted store values without waiting for hydration to complete.

missing_context_questions: Does the theme need to be applied before first paint, or can a brief flash of the default theme be tolerated?
Is the theme stored in a cookie that could be read server-side to eliminate the mismatch?
target_report.repair_prompt: Please inspect src/components/ThemeWrapper.tsx and the Zustand store. Hydration fails because the server renders 'theme-light' but client rehydrates 'theme-dark' from localStorage. Use Zustand's skipHydration option: 'persist(storeConfig, { name: "theme", skipHydration: true })'. Then in a client component, call 'useThemeStore.persist.rehydrate()' inside a useEffect. This delays localStorage reads until after React hydration. Alternatively, store the theme in a cookie and read it server-side for consistent SSR.
verification_steps: Add 'skipHydration: true' to the Zustand persist config.
Call 'useThemeStore.persist.rehydrate()' inside a useEffect in a client component.
Test with a persisted 'dark' theme: load the page and verify no hydration error appears in console.

review.review_notes: Synthetic fetch no-cors mode returning opaque response with no readable body.

context.recent_changes: Attempted to call a third-party API directly from the browser to bypass a CORS error.

reference_annotations.reference_cause: Using mode: 'no-cors' produces an opaque response whose body cannot be read in JavaScript. It is not a CORS solution — it just silences the error while making the response unreadable.
reference_annotations.reference_repair: Remove mode: 'no-cors' and proxy the API call through your own backend, or use a third-party proxy if the API supports it.

target_report.summary: mode: 'no-cors' produces an opaque response with no readable body, making it impossible to parse the API JSON.
target_report.plain_explanation: The 'no-cors' fetch mode is not a CORS workaround. It silences the browser CORS error, but as a security measure, the browser gives you an 'opaque' response — you can confirm the request went out but cannot read the status code, headers, or body. The correct fix for CORS is to proxy the request through your own backend, where there is no same-origin restriction.

likely_causes.description: mode: 'no-cors' was added to silence a CORS error, without understanding that it makes the response unreadable.
The third-party API does not send CORS headers, so direct browser requests are blocked.

missing_context_questions: Do you have control over the third-party API to add CORS headers?
Can a backend route in your application proxy this request to the third-party API?
warnings: Never use mode: 'no-cors' expecting to read the response; it is intended only for fire-and-forget requests like analytics beacons.
target_report.repair_prompt: Please inspect the fetch call to 'https://api.third-party.com/data'. Using mode: 'no-cors' is incorrect here. Remove the no-cors mode and instead create a server-side proxy route in your backend (e.g. Next.js API route at '/api/proxy/data') that fetches from the third-party API using node-fetch or the built-in fetch. Your frontend then calls '/api/proxy/data' on your own domain, avoiding CORS entirely. Do not use mode: 'no-cors' to read response data.
verification_steps: Create a proxy API route in your backend that fetches from the third-party API.
Update the frontend fetch call to use your proxy endpoint instead of the third-party URL.
Verify the response body is readable and contains the expected JSON data.

review.review_notes: Synthetic React context causing excessive re-renders on all consumers.

context.recent_changes: Moved all global state into a single AppContext provider.

reference_annotations.reference_cause: A single large context causes all consumers to re-render whenever any part of the context value changes, even if the consumer only uses an unrelated slice.
reference_annotations.reference_repair: Split the monolithic context into smaller focused contexts (UserContext, ThemeContext, CartContext) so consumers only re-render when their relevant data changes.

target_report.summary: All React components re-render on every state change because a single large context holds all global state.
target_report.plain_explanation: React Context re-renders every consumer component whenever the context value changes. When all global state (user, theme, cart, notifications, settings) is in one context object, a cart update causes user profile components to re-render, and a notification triggers cart components to re-render — even though the relevant data didn't change for those components.

likely_causes.description: A monolithic AppContext combines unrelated state slices, causing all consumers to re-render on any change.
The context value object is recreated on every parent render, triggering reference equality failures even when data is unchanged.

missing_context_questions: How many components consume the AppContext?
Are there independent slices of state that could be split into separate contexts?
target_report.repair_prompt: Please inspect AppContext and its consumers. React Profiler shows excessive re-renders because all state is in one context. Split into focused contexts: 'UserContext', 'CartContext', 'ThemeContext', etc. Each component then subscribes only to the context it needs. Also wrap context values in useMemo to prevent unnecessary reference changes: 'const userValue = useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user]);'. For complex global state, consider Zustand or Jotai which provide selector-based subscriptions.
verification_steps: Split AppContext into smaller, focused context providers.
Verify each consuming component only re-renders when its specific context slice changes.
Use React DevTools Profiler to confirm render counts decrease significantly.

review.review_notes: Synthetic async function in array.map returning array of Promises instead of resolved values.

context.recent_changes: Added async processing to a batch operation using Array.map.

reference_annotations.reference_cause: Array.map does not await async callbacks; each callback returns a Promise immediately, so the map result is an array of unresolved Promises.
reference_annotations.reference_repair: Wrap with Promise.all: 'const processedItems = await Promise.all(items.map(async (item) => processItem(item)));'

target_report.summary: Array.map with an async callback returns an array of Promises, not resolved values; Promise.all is needed.
target_report.plain_explanation: JavaScript's Array.map is synchronous. When the callback is an async function, map returns immediately with an array of Promise objects — one per item. The Promises are still pending. To wait for all of them to resolve, you must wrap the map call with 'await Promise.all(...)'.

likely_causes.description: Array.map was used with an async callback without wrapping in Promise.all.
The calling function or code path does not await the result of the map.

missing_context_questions: Should items be processed in parallel (Promise.all) or sequentially (for...of with await)?
What is the acceptable level of concurrency for processItem?
warnings: Promise.all runs all promises concurrently; if processItem has side effects or hits rate limits, consider processing items sequentially with a for...of loop and await inside.
target_report.repair_prompt: Please update the batch processing code. 'items.map(async ...)' returns an array of Promises, not resolved values. Wrap with Promise.all: 'const processedItems = await Promise.all(items.map(async (item) => processItem(item)));'. If sequential processing is needed (to avoid overwhelming a database or API), use: 'const processedItems = []; for (const item of items) { processedItems.push(await processItem(item)); }'.
verification_steps: Replace 'items.map(async ...)' with 'await Promise.all(items.map(async ...))'.
Log processedItems[0] and verify it shows the resolved value, not a Promise object.
Run a test with a small item array and confirm all results are correctly resolved.

review.review_notes: Synthetic file upload FormData boundary stripped when manually setting Content-Type header.

context.recent_changes: Added a file upload endpoint using multer on Express.

reference_annotations.reference_cause: Manually setting 'Content-Type: multipart/form-data' overwrites the browser's auto-generated header that includes the multipart boundary string. Without the boundary, the server cannot parse the form data.
reference_annotations.reference_repair: Remove the 'Content-Type' header from the fetch options and let the browser set it automatically with the correct boundary.

target_report.summary: File upload failed because manually setting Content-Type overwrote the browser's multipart boundary in the header.
target_report.plain_explanation: When you send a FormData object with fetch, the browser automatically sets the 'Content-Type' header to 'multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary...'. The boundary is a unique string the server uses to separate the different parts of the upload. By manually setting 'Content-Type: multipart/form-data' (without a boundary), you overwrite the browser's auto-generated header and the server cannot parse the multipart body.

likely_causes.description: Content-Type: multipart/form-data was manually added to fetch headers, stripping the required boundary parameter.
A generic request interceptor (Axios defaults, a middleware) is overriding the Content-Type header for all POST requests.

missing_context_questions: Is there an Axios interceptor or fetch wrapper that automatically adds a Content-Type header to all requests?
Are you using Axios instead of fetch? Axios has a separate fix for FormData uploads.
target_report.repair_prompt: Please inspect the fetch call in the file upload handler. Express/multer throws: "Boundary not found". Remove the 'Content-Type' header from the fetch options entirely: 'await fetch("/api/upload", { method: "POST", body: formData });'. The browser will automatically set the correct multipart Content-Type with boundary. If using Axios, delete the Content-Type from default headers for this request: 'axios.post("/api/upload", formData, { headers: { "Content-Type": undefined } })'.
verification_steps: Remove the 'Content-Type' header from the fetch options.
Upload a file and verify the request headers in browser DevTools show the boundary parameter.
Confirm the Express/multer endpoint receives and processes the file successfully.
